name: Colin Moreau

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We don't sell anything or campaign for any side, and this conversation is confidential. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Colin, 27, and I lead rewiring and repair work in older homes and small commercial buildings. I've a two-year technical diploma and a master electrician's licence, and the firm pays me above the usual rate for untangling other people's awkward jobs. I live alone, have nine months of expenses saved, and could approach plenty of electrical employers nearby without moving. I use a paper diary and don't use AI at all; finding a hidden junction is satisfying, but being told to replace a working method with another screen makes me tired before I've started.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that sounds quite sensible, if the useful bits stay useful. Nobody needs to announce a new age because an office letter takes less time. I'd rather hear that the job address is right and the cable order has arrived.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My wage and savings feel solid in that picture. I've nine months of costs covered, no dependants, and a skill other local firms still pay for. I'd have no reason to disturb a working arrangement just because the big prediction turned out smaller.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my repair and rewiring rota, paper diary and existing test records throughout the next year. This month I'd book the usual check of my test meter, using the ordinary equipment allowance. Otherwise I'd leave my savings where they are and carry on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a little amused at the size of the noise compared with the result. I wouldn't feel cheated out of a revolution. I'd enjoy being able to plan an ordinary week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is the first thing you check on an older building?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start with the board labels and the readings, not the age of the building alone. A neatly written label can still be wrong. Familiar tools are useful because I know their limits, not because I think old things never fail.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever consider changing a working method?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask whether the new method solves a particular problem and whether someone has tested the result. I'd listen to that answer. I wouldn't volunteer for an AI trial just to show I'm a cooperative person.

say: I'd welcome **useful modest changes** without announcing a new age over faster office letters.
I'd focus on **correct job details** and materials reaching the site.
think: My **wage and savings** feel solid, with nine months covered and no dependants.
Nearby employers still pay for my **electrical skill**, so I needn't disturb a working arrangement.
do: Keep the **repair rota** and paper diary through the next year.
Book the test meter's **usual check** this month from the equipment allowance.
feel: **Calm and settled**, pleased to plan an ordinary week without needing a technological revolution.
S0.quote: I wouldn't feel cheated out of a revolution.
fieldNote: His **strong reserve** and plentiful local employers support calm rather than merely a composed speaking style.
His caution about **labels and limits** shows that resistance to AI does not mean unquestioning trust in familiar equipment.

steps.text: Keep electrical repairs, paper diary and routine meter checks

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say let the office deal with the booking software, and show me the result in a reliable day's schedule. I'm not going to call a tool useless without looking at what comes out. I'm also not going to pretend I want to use it myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my own paid hours are secure for now because most of my work happens inside a building with test leads in my hands. It still unsettles me when a new schedule starts deciding how long a difficult job ought to take. My savings mean I can question that without worrying about next week's food.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask my manager to keep giving me a printed schedule during the changeover. For the first year I'd continue the rewiring work and note any difference between estimated and actual site time on the paper job sheet. After two months I'd take those records to the manager and ask for corrections if the allowances were wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, though not worried that my own income is about to vanish. I like knowing who to phone when a job runs over. A screen with a cheerful finish time isn't a person who can explain the delay to a customer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What details would you record about a late job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd write down whether the delay came from access, a wrong record or an extra fault. I'd want the reason attached, not just a larger number beside my name. If the new schedule worked well, I'd record that too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn the AI scheduling system?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd listen to a printed explanation of the changed process, but I'd leave operating the AI to the office. If something required me personally to use it, I'd ask what alternative existed before agreeing. I don't pick up a new system quickly, and pretending otherwise would help nobody.

say: I'd judge **reliable schedules** rather than dismiss every new tool before seeing its output.
I'd tell colleagues plainly that I don't want to **operate AI** myself.
think: My own **near-term hours** look secure because rewiring and testing remain hands-on.
I'm unsettled by **software time allowances**, even though savings let me question them safely.
do: Request a **printed schedule** during the changeover now.
Continue rewiring and record **actual site time** on paper through the first year.
Review the records with the manager after **two months** and request corrections if needed.
feel: **Uneasy about control**, while expecting his own income to remain secure for now.
S1.quote: A screen with a cheerful finish time isn't a person who can explain the delay to a customer.
fieldNote: He draws a clear line between **judging output** and learning to operate an AI system himself.
His mood follows **secure personal hours** alongside disruption to familiar control of the working day, rather than assumed job loss.

steps.text: Continue rewiring with paper records of actual and estimated site time

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say 2028 changes the thinking side, and around 2031 the capable robots can reach the work I do with my hands. I wouldn't tell the younger apprentice that a licence settles the question. I'd ask the firm to say what it's actually buying before any of us makes a grand plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My hours could shrink sharply once capable robots spread, even though I might find work at another local firm. Nine months in the bank gives me time to check, not immunity. I'd worry about using the whole reserve while waiting for the old pattern to return.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'd postpone the motorcycle I planned to buy and add the 200 monthly purchase saving to my emergency account instead. During 2029 I'd speak to three local electrical firms about posted repair vacancies and their actual equipment orders. I'd apply for steadier work if it existed, leaving only with written basic hours and pay that covered my bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I can still picture several choices before panic. I wouldn't be deciding with an empty account. The difficult part would be admitting that waiting for a familiar answer might use up the money that gives me those choices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you judge a nearby firm's offer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd compare actual hours, travel and the sort of repairs, not just take the friendliest owner's word. A firm that promised endless work without discussing the machines would worry me. I want a wage agreement, not a comforting story.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you spend part of the reserve on learning AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I wouldn't buy an AI course in the first rush of fear. I'd ask an experienced training adviser about options only if the repair search produced nothing suitable. I know that's slower than some people would move, but I wouldn't claim an enquiry was a new career.

say: I'd distinguish **2028 thinking work** from capable robots reaching physical repairs around 2031.
I'd ask what the firm is **actually buying**, without claiming the licence settles our future.
think: My **hours could shrink** when capable robots spread, even with other local employers to approach.
Nine months saved gives me **checking time**, but waiting for familiar work could exhaust it.
do: Redirect **200 monthly** from the postponed motorcycle purchase into emergency savings now.
Contact **three local firms** in 2029 about posted repair vacancies and real equipment orders.
Change jobs only for **written basic terms** covering hours, pay and household bills.
feel: **Anxious with choices**, aware that money can disappear while he waits for familiar answers.
S2.quote: I want a wage agreement, not a comforting story.
fieldNote: He acknowledges **personal income risk** despite substantial reserves and plentiful employers, which do not guarantee future vacancies.
Any **training enquiry** remains a fallback question; neither AI learning nor course enrolment is claimed as an action.

steps.text: Save the motorcycle purchase contribution of 200 monthly for emergencies
Seek posted repair work in 2029 with bill-covering written pay and hours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the extra years give a cautious person time to see which promises turn into work. Thinking AI arrives in 2031 and capable robots around 2034. I'd use the gap to check employers, not call it proof that nothing reaches our trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't expect my basic wage to disappear in the next few years, and the reserve is strong. I'm still uneasy about what happens when machines do the physical repairs, because at 32 in 2031 I'm nowhere near finished earning. I'd have more room than in the fast picture to compare actual options without resigning first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd redirect the 200 motorcycle contribution into emergency savings for a year, then review the balance. Each autumn I'd check real electrical vacancies and ask about ordinary paid hours while keeping my current job. In 2032 I'd apply to any demonstrably steadier repair firm, but only move for written terms covering my bills and travel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, rather than expecting an immediate blow to my own wage. I can give myself time to ask the same question twice and see whether the answer changes. That suits me better than acting because everybody else looks busy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you postpone the motorcycle for all five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd review it after a year instead of turning the motorcycle into a symbol of all future danger. If the reserve and booked work remained strong, I'd decide whether the purchase still made sense. If hours weakened, the money would stay available for bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What evidence would make another firm look steadier?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask whether the advertised hours had actually been paid through the last quiet period. I'd also ask what equipment had been ordered, because a vacancy today doesn't tell me the firm's next plan. I wouldn't demand certainty, just something I could check.

say: I'd say **extra years** allow cautious checking of promises against actual paid work.
I'd keep the **2031 and 2034** changes distinct without claiming electricians remain untouched.
think: My **near-term basic wage** and reserve look secure, but later physical automation stays on my mind.
At **32 in 2031**, I'll still need many years of earnings and cannot rely on retirement.
do: Redirect **200 monthly** into emergency savings for one year before reviewing the motorcycle purchase.
Keep current repairs while checking **actual vacancies** each autumn.
Apply in **2032** to steadier firms only on bill-covering written terms including travel costs.
feel: **Uneasy with breathing room**, able to check offers slowly while continuing to earn.
S3.quote: I wouldn't demand certainty, just something I could check.
fieldNote: His milder mood rests on **secure near-term wages**, with later risk acknowledged rather than removed by confidence alone.
The saving choice has a **one-year review**; later applications retain checks on actual paid hours, equipment orders and written terms.

steps.text: Save the 200 motorcycle contribution monthly for one year before reviewing
Seek demonstrably steadier repair work in 2032 with bill-covering written terms

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years gives us room to keep working and pay attention without turning every week into an emergency. I'd ask the firm for an annual conversation about orders and equipment. I wouldn't sign up for ten years of courses because somebody put a robot on a leaflet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own income looks safe over the next few years in this picture, with a good wage and a reserve behind it. At 37 in 2036 I'll still need work, and robots around 2039 could change that work a great deal. I'm uneasy about the later question, but I don't need to answer it by leaving a good job now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the present repairs and set an annual diary reminder to review savings, booked hours and equipment orders. I'd redirect the 200 monthly motorcycle contribution for the first year, then review instead of promising the same saving for a decade. During 2037 I'd apply for a genuinely steadier repair vacancy if one existed, moving only with written pay and hours covering my bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but with space for an ordinary life around the concern. I'd still go out with friends and spend an evening fixing my old radio. Keeping an eye on the future doesn't mean staring at it all day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you change the annual review date?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd bring the review forward if my paid hours fell or the firm placed an actual machine order that changed staffing. A video alone wouldn't be enough. I'd ask what was going to happen to our rota and write down the answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you rule out all future study?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look at practical courses only when I could name the work they led toward and check the demand. That doesn't mean I'd never learn again. It means I wouldn't spend money on a new identity before finding out whether anybody paid for that work.

say: I'd describe **ten years** as room to work and pay attention without treating every week as an emergency.
I'd seek an **annual work discussion** instead of buying courses from frightening advertising.
think: My **near-term income** looks secure because of good pay, available work and substantial savings.
At **37 in 2036**, I'll still need future earnings, so later robots remain a serious question.
do: Keep **current repairs** with annual checks of savings, paid hours and actual equipment orders.
Redirect **200 monthly** into emergency savings for one year before reviewing.
Seek genuinely steadier vacancies in **2037** only if written pay and hours cover household bills.
feel: **Uneasy but unhurried**, leaving room for friends and familiar hobbies alongside annual checks.
S4.quote: Keeping an eye on the future doesn't mean staring at it all day.
fieldNote: The long warning preserves **present security** without being mistaken for retirement protection or a guarantee of later repair demand.
He remains resistant to speculative study while leaving future **practical learning** open; no unsupported retraining tag is added.

steps.text: Continue electrical repairs with annual savings, hours and equipment reviews
Save 200 monthly for one year before reviewing the motorcycle purchase
Seek genuinely steadier repair work in 2037 on bill-covering written terms

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because robots around 2031 could reduce my hours before I've checked a steadier route. I'd want honest notice of staffing plans and someone independent who could explain actual job and training options without selling a course. Nine months of savings buys questions, not a guaranteed answer.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether I like being known for doing the job properly. I do, and losing that place in a team would hurt even if I could pay the bills for a while. Money gives me time to decide; it doesn't decide what I'd want to be useful for.

headlineQuote: Nine months of savings buys questions, not a guaranteed answer.
portrait: At **27**, Colin leads electrical repairs with a technical diploma and master licence, higher pay, and nine months of expenses saved.
He lives **alone**, has no dependants, and can approach plenty of nearby electrical employers without moving home.
He avoids **AI tools**, prefers paper methods, and tests practical claims rather than choosing a political side.
Fast change makes him **anxious** about hours; longer warnings support cautious vacancy checks without assuming future wages or buying speculative training.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could reduce his hours when capable robots follow around 2031 before he has checked a steadier route.
whatWouldHelp: **Honest staffing notice** and independent advice on actual jobs and training would help him compare options without a course sales pitch.
